settings.title: Stops cluster in the obvious spots
settings.text: Under the swing low, over the range high, on the round number — because that's what every guide taught.

settings.title: A cluster of stops is a pool of liquidity
settings.text: Resting orders are fuel. To fill size, price has to trade into where those orders sit.

settings.title: You enter without a filter
settings.text: You chase the move into the level — the same level everyone's stop is leaning on.

settings.title: Price sweeps, then reverses
settings.text: The pool gets taken, your stop is part of it, and the real move happens without you.

settings.label: 1 · Sweep
settings.text: A resting liquidity pool gets taken.

settings.label: 3 · Agree
settings.text: ES and NQ both tell the same story.

settings.rule: A clear liquidity sweep has occurred (a known pool was taken).
Price rejects the swept level rather than accepting through it.
A break of structure prints in your direction.
An inverse FVG (fair value gap) flips to support your side.
ES and NQ agree — no divergence pulling against you.
Entry, stop and target are defined before you click.
The setup sits inside your session and time window.
You have taken zero revenge or 'make-it-back' trades today.

settings.question: Another system? Seen one, seen 'em all.
settings.answer: Most 'systems' add another way to find trades. This does the opposite — it's a filter that removes trades. If you already have setups you like, keep them; the gate just decides which ones you're allowed to take.

settings.question: Why pay when everything's free on YouTube?
settings.answer: Because the problem was never a shortage of information. You already know more than enough to trade. What's missing is one written, pre-committed rule you'll actually follow — assembled in one place instead of scattered across 40 hours of videos you'll never re-watch.

settings.question: Does this work live, or just on demo?
settings.answer: The whole design assumption is that live is where discipline breaks. That's why the decision is made before the click, in writing — so the hard part isn't left to a stressed version of you. And you're told to backtest it on your own data first, so you're not finding out live.

settings.question: It looks too simple to be worth £35.
settings.answer: It is simple. That's the feature, not a bug — a rule you can run under pressure has to be simple. The value isn't complexity, it's the specific gate and the fact that you'll actually use it.

settings.question: I'll just break these rules too.
settings.answer: Maybe. A written gate won't chain your hands. But it does two things willpower can't: it makes breaking the rule a conscious choice you have to see yourself make, and it gives you a clean record of what happens when you do. Most people don't need more force — they need to stop lying to themselves in the moment.

settings.question: I'm not really a maths person.
settings.answer: There's no maths to be good at. The gate is a checklist of yes/no market conditions, in plain English. If you can read a chart well enough to lose money on it, you can read it well enough to run the filter.

settings.question: If it worked, you'd trade it — not sell it.
settings.answer: Reasonable suspicion. The honest version is in the founder note above: this is a process, not a profit machine, and it's sold as a one-off written kit — not a signal group I need you to renew. Read the risk warning; there are no income claims here on purpose.

settings.question: Does this even apply to me — I trade stocks, not ES/NQ?
settings.answer: It's written specifically for ES and NASDAQ intraday. The idea of filtering entries around liquidity is more general, but the exact rules, sessions and the ES/NQ agreement check are built for those two instruments. If you don't trade them, be honest with yourself about the fit before buying.
